1:
The purpose of the section gets settled before anything in it is described. Gill reads it as the rites and rules for presenting one: who had to bring a trespass offering was laid down in the two preceding chapters, ignorant and deliberate sinners alike, while these verses declare the place, the parts, and their disposal. Ellicott would render the opening simply and this is the law, and reads these ten verses as doing for the trespass what the close of the previous chapter did for the sin offering — furnishing the priest with instructions more precise than the earlier law gave him. Keil and Delitzsch call the directions about burnt and meat offerings further on an appendix, misplaced here and properly belonging among the older laws for those sacrifices.

The killing is fixed by cross-reference rather than described. Clarke and Ellicott both place it on the north side of the altar, and Ellicott adds that the subject of the verb is the people bringing the sacrifice, since the offerers themselves slaughtered the victim. For the blood he would read throw rather than sprinkle, and marks a divergence from the sin offering: there it went on the horns, here it was flung against the walls, or round about. Keil and Delitzsch let the likeness to the burnt offering at this point carry over into significance as well as procedure.

The scarlet line comes in from two directions at once. Ellicott reports a scarlet thread running round the altar at exactly its middle during the second Temple, the blood of trespass and peace offerings being thrown below the line and that of a whole burnt sacrifice above it; Henry has the tradition too, by way of bishop Patrick, and puts it to the same use.

Of the parts burnt, Gill notes that the fat was claimed by God as in the peace offerings of herd and flock and the sin offering of the bullock, and that the kidneys are named because they are usually covered with it. Clarke sends the reader back to the earlier chapter for the rump and the rest, the principal subjects being nearly identical in both. Keil and Delitzsch make the parallel exact: only fat portions went up in smoke, as in the sin and peace offerings, while the flesh fell to the priests, as there — one law governing both, every trespass being a sin, and hence an identical significance in these parts of the service.

Henry draws the practical consequence. Being much of one nature with the sin offering, the trespass fell under identical rules, and the offerer got no share: it was divided entirely between altar and priest, where a man did partake of his own peace offering. He takes the difference for fitness rather than arbitrariness. Peace offerings were brought in thankfulness for mercy, and feasting suited them; a trespass was brought in sorrow for sin, and fasting suited that better, in token of holy mourning and of a resolution to abstain from what had been repented of.

He finds a further encouragement in the arrangement. The flesh belonged to the priest who had presented it, so the readier a man was at the altar the more he got — wages following work, and the same rule holding in religion, that the more diligent we are the more we reap. Nor did the perquisite stay with one man: any of the priests, and the males of their households, might be invited to share it, and Henry supposes they treated one another out of these dues, so that fellowship was kept up among them.
5:
Gill and Ellicott dispose of the burning quickly, since it has been described already: the fat taken from the parts just named, together with the kidneys, was what the priest burnt, exactly as in the sin offering and the peace offering. What was left of the flesh, Gill notes, belonged to the priests and their sons, and to them only — not to their wives and daughters.

Calvin treats the passage as confirming the priests' rights already established and adding an exception not raised before. In general it gives the priests whatever remained of the holier victims, and by that prerogative distinguishes them from the rest of the Levites; from which he draws a point about the lawgiver rather than the law. Moses, at God's command, was depriving his own sons not only of the dignity conferred on his nephews but of the money that went with it, which Calvin takes as a proof of how free from self-seeking he was.

The special provision is aimed at rivalry inside the priesthood. Since some might have arisen, certain kinds of offering were reserved to the priest who had actually presented them — the residue of the peace offerings, the right shoulder, and the flesh left over from the trespass offerings all going to the man who performed the atonement and sprinkled the blood. Calvin does not pretend this is the higher motive. They ought all to have discharged their duties disinterestedly, without being drawn by lucre; but a reward was appointed for their labour and diligence so that every one of them might perform his part more cheerfully. Many, he grants, were doubtless drawn by the desire of gain who would otherwise have neglected the work, and that God should consult their infirmity so far as to make their hire a spur to their diligence he calls an instance of fatherly indulgence.

What God did not want, on the same reading, was mercenaries in heart. When the prophet reproves the priests because not one of them would kindle fire on the altar for nothing, Calvin takes the aggravation to lie deeper than their refusal to serve gratis: having received their hire, they defrauded the one who had appointed them his ministers.

On the clause that makes one law for the sin offering and the trespass offering, Ellicott draws out the working consequence — what is omitted from the regulations of the one must be supplied from the directions given for the other. Wesley narrows the scope before it can be over-read: the two are one law in the matter immediately following, since in other things they differed; and what the priest was to have was the part of it God had allowed him.
8:
Why the skin is singled out has a plain answer and an elaborate one. Gill gives the plain one: in the burnt offering the flesh was wholly consumed, so nothing remained to requite the priest for his trouble as in the other offerings. Ellicott gives the same reason and then the later practice built on it — under the rule that obtained in the second Temple the skins of the most holy things went to the officiating priests, while those of the holy things, the peace offerings, belonged to the owners of the victims; the skins accumulated through the week, and the course whose turn it was to serve divided them among themselves every Sabbath evening.

Clarke reaches much further back, following bishop Patrick. The priest's right to the skin is traced to the first sacrifice of all: Adam, probably, offered it, and God gave him the skin to clothe himself and his wife, in conformity with which the priests ever after had the skin of the whole burnt offering for their portion. The Gentiles kept the same custom, giving the skins of their sacrifices to their priests where they were not burnt with the victim — and put them to a use Clarke takes to be superstitious, lying upon them in the temples in hope that things to come would be revealed in dreams. His witness is Virgil, whose priest sleeps on the fleeces of slaughtered sheep in the silent night, sees thin airy forms flying before him, hears voices, and talks familiarly with the gods; and whose king, wanting an answer, kills a hundred sheep, lies down on their skins, and hears the god reply out of the wood.

The same practice, Clarke says, survived into his own time in the Highlands of Scotland, and he sets down the account at length. A man was wrapped in the hide of a newly killed bullock and left beside a waterfall, or at the foot of a precipice, or in some other place where the scenery suggested nothing but objects of horror; there he turned the question over in his mind through the night, and whatever his imagination impressed on him passed for the inspiration of the spirits that haunt such recesses, his companions returning at daybreak for the answer. Clarke reports one man of the Isle of Lewis who had spent such a night under the hide and felt and heard things he could not express, and who said that for a thousand worlds he would never be concerned in the like again.

The meat offerings are divided on a different principle, and Wesley supplies the reason. Whatever had been baked in the oven or dressed in the pan went, apart from the memorial burnt on the altar, to the particular priest who offered it, since the man who laboured about it might in reason expect something more than his brethren who did not; and that was the only offering in which he had it. Raw flour was the exception. Ellicott would read the clause as or dry rather than and, covering the flour offering mingled with oil, the poor man's sin offering which had no oil put on it, and the offering of jealousy, all of which were shared equally among the sons of Aaron. Wesley's reason for the difference is practical: these were in greater quantity, and being raw could more easily be kept for each priest to dress in the way he liked. Ellicott adds a note on the words a man as his brother, absent from the English but present in the Hebrew, from which the later rule was drawn that no child or woman of priestly descent might share in this offering, while a priest disqualified from officiating by a bodily blemish might, since he still came under the designation of a man.
11:
Gill treats the heading as an announcement of what is still outstanding. What the peace offerings were to be, of the herd and of the flock, and how their fat was to be burnt, had been settled already; what follows distinguishes the several sorts, prescribes what was to be offered along with them, marks the priest's share, and fixes when the flesh might be eaten. Ellicott places the section in the same pattern he has traced twice before — as the sin offering and the trespass offering each received fuller directions for the priests after the people had been instructed, so here. He also flags a Hebrew idiom in the clause that follows: the verb has a subject with no antecedent, and English carries it better as an impersonal or a passive, which one shall offer, or which shall be offered.

Three classes are then distinguished, and Henry gives each its occasion. The first is thankfulness for a special mercy received — recovery from sickness, preservation on a journey, deliverance at sea, redemption out of captivity, the very list for which men are called on to offer the sacrifice of thanksgiving in the hundred and seventh Psalm. The second is the performance of a vow made in distress, which he reckons less honourable than the first, though the omission of it would have been more culpable. The third is supplication for some mercy a man was still in pursuit of, the voluntary offering, which accompanied his prayers as the first accompanied his praises.

What Henry finds most worth remarking is that none of the three was commanded. A man was not bound by law to bring a peace offering on any of these occasions unless he had bound himself by a vow, where the sacrifices of atonement were required of him whenever he sinned. Not, he is careful to say, that prayer and praise are less our duty than repentance; but in the expressions of their sense of mercy God left them more at liberty than in the expressions of their sense of sin — partly to try the generosity of their devotion, so that sacrifices which were freewill offerings might be the more laudable and acceptable, and partly because in obliging them to bring the offerings of atonement he was showing the necessity of the great propitiation.

Calvin builds his name for the whole class out of the same breadth of occasion. He calls them the sacrifices of prosperities, since they were brought not only in token of gratitude but when God's aid was being implored, and since in every case the offerer was acknowledging God as the author of all good things — whether he was returning thanks for some notable blessing, seeking deliverance from danger, professing his piety in general, or paying a vow made simply and without condition. Even a conditional vow paid, he observes, was itself an act of thanksgiving. The name is therefore justly given: in these offerings men either besought good success from God, or owned that what they had already obtained came from his grace, or asked relief in adversity, or congratulated themselves on their safety. Out of the class so described Moses then marks off one kind in particular, the sacrifice of thanksgiving, by which a man professedly returned thanks for some notable deliverance — and which, unlike the rest, was not always offered.
12:
How wide the occasion for thanksgiving ran is disputed among the authorities Gill cites. Jarchi confines it to the more wonderful deliverances — of seafaring men, of travellers, of prisoners, of those who had lain under violent disease — and Aben Ezra likewise seems to understand it only of being brought out of distress; but Gill will not narrow it that far, allowing it for the common mercies of life, or for any particular instance of divine goodness a man was sensible of and thought fit to acknowledge this way. Ellicott gives the narrower list, drawn from the same Psalm, and takes this to be the sacrifice the apostle has in view where he bids us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually.

The accompanying bread is prescribed in four kinds, and the quantities are not. Ellicott infers from that silence that the amounts were left to those who administered the law and guided the people, and reports what the second Temple settled on: the offerer brought twenty pottles of fine flour, made ten of them into ten leavened cakes, and out of the other ten made thirty unleavened, using half a log of oil — ten baked in the oven, ten made into wafers, ten hastily fried. All of them, he adds, had to be baked before the victim was killed.

The leavened bread is the anomaly, and it is defended rather than explained away. Wesley grants that leaven was forbidden, but confines the prohibition to what was offered and burnt on the altar, which this bread was not; and he finds the reason for it in the occasion, this being a thanksgiving for God's blessings, among which leavened bread was itself one. Ellicott notes that the only other offering to include it was at Pentecost, and that there too no part of it went on the altar as a memorial. Keil and Delitzsch fill in what the text leaves unsaid: a memorial portion of the unleavened pastry was burnt, as the earlier law required, while none of the leavened cake was placed on the altar at all but simply served as bread for the sacrificial meal.

Of the whole oblation one piece was lifted out for God. Gill takes it to mean one from each sort, and cites Aben Ezra for four at the least, and Maimonides for the priest taking one out of every kind. Ellicott would render the clause one out of each outright, and does the arithmetic: the officiating priest waved four loaves, one of every sort, and kept them, the remaining thirty-six going to the owner of the sacrifice. Keil and Delitzsch specify which priest — the one who had sprinkled the blood of the peace offering. Wesley finds the arrangement the most agreeable to the rules laid down elsewhere, since it gives the priest a share in the unleavened cakes and wafers as well as in the leavened bread.

The flesh of a thanksgiving offering had to be finished the same day. Keil and Delitzsch set the rule against the looser one for vows and freewill offerings, which might be eaten on the second day as well. Clarke offers two reasons and prefers neither: in so hot a country the flesh was apt to putrefy, and it would have been improper to expose to putrefaction what had been consecrated; or else, on Harmer's suggestion, the law is aimed at the custom of drying devoted flesh, still practised among the Mohammedans, which might be turned to superstitious use. Ellicott reads the limit as designed: the offerer, his family and his poor guests had to eat it up before morning — midnight, by the reckoning of the second Temple — which both encouraged liberality to the poor and kept the meal recognisably a sacred feast rather than an occasion for unseemly conviviality.
16:
What marks off the second class from the first is disputed, and the two accounts are not compatible. Ellicott takes the distinction to lie between the vow and the freewill offering themselves, as the canon law of a later age drew it: a vow is an obligation a man lays on himself in the words behold, I take it upon myself to bring a bullock for a peace offering, and it binds him until he fulfils it, so that if the beast dies or is stolen or becomes disqualified he must bring another; a freewill offering pledges only the particular animal, behold, this animal I devote, so that if that animal dies or is stolen the obligation lapses with it. Calvin reads the passage as being about a different distinction altogether. What is meant here, he argues, is not a conditional vow but a simple one — for a man who had vowed on condition and obtained what he asked was paying an act of thanksgiving, and his sacrifice would fall under the first head already dealt with; it would be absurd to distinguish things that do not differ. Because many made gratuitous vows, Moses ranks this kind with the freewill offering as standing on the same footing.

Why these two were allowed an extra day is answered by their occasion. Ellicott makes both an indirect mode of supplication with an eye to favours still to come, and so not the spontaneous expression of devotion that the thank offering was; being less sacred, they might be eaten on the day of presentation and on the day after. Wesley marks the same permission simply as something not allowed for the thank offering.

Calvin gives two reasons for there being any limit at all. The consecrated meats were not to be kept so long that they turned and religion fell into contempt; and perhaps, he adds, vainglory was being guarded against, since if a man had been free to salt the flesh and eat it at leisure many would have made ostentatious offerings at no real expense — so God imposed a restraint, that they might offer more sparingly and more reverently. Gill and Ellicott account for the third-day remainder in plainer terms: what was left uneaten on the second day and kept over had to be burnt, and Ellicott notes the two ways a surplus arose — either the sacrifice was very plentiful, or the owner was too niggardly to invite poor guests enough to finish it.

The penalty falls on the offerer as much as on the eater. Ellicott makes him responsible for seeing the rule kept: if through his neglect anyone ate after the limit, the efficacy of the sacrifice was cancelled and he had to bring another votive offering. The word rendered abomination he explains from the climate, flesh left that long beginning to putrefy and so desecrating what was holy, with the eater reckoned as eating carrion and incurring excision. Keil and Delitzsch make the philological point behind it: the term is used of sacrificial flesh and of nothing else, and properly signifies a stench.

On the clause about imputing, Calvin turns the negative round. If polluted sacrifices are not reckoned to a man, it follows that sacrifices duly offered do come into account before God, who counts them as expended on himself — though we are not to imagine them merits that lay him under obligation, but rather that he deals so liberally with us that no duty paid him is wasted. Wesley reads the same clause more narrowly, as meaning that the offering will not stand as an acceptable service.
19:
The flesh could be spoiled by contact as well as by keeping. Gill and Ellicott both take the case to be one that might easily arise on the way from the altar to the house or tent where the meal was held: a person ceremonially unclean, a woman under her separation, someone who had touched a defiled thing, or an animal such as a dog, might touch the flesh in transit, and it then had to be burnt rather than eaten, so that no profane use was made of it. The corresponding permission Ellicott would render every one that is clean may eat the flesh — that is, anyone the offerer invited might share in the meal, provided he was legally clean. Wesley narrows the general word carefully: it is the holy offering that is meant, other flesh being unaffected; and he infers from the fact that the offerers and their guests ate it that the meal did not take place in the holy place, since they could not go there.

The second case reverses the first. Keil and Delitzsch set out the ground of the sentence: the man who eats of the peace offering with his uncleanness upon him is to be cut off, whether the defilement came from touching an unclean object, or from the uncleanness of a man, or from an unclean beast, or from any other unclean abomination — a term which takes in the unclean fishes, birds and smaller creatures. Clarke glosses the phrase about having his uncleanness upon him as meaning a man who had touched something defiling and had not since washed his clothes and bathed. Wesley separates the two verses by the source of the defilement, the first speaking of uncleanness arising within a man and the second of what came from without; and he limits the penalty to the man who ate knowingly, since a sacrifice was accepted for what was done in ignorance.

Gill and Clarke fill in what those uncleannesses were. Gill lists the dead body of a man, a bone of one, or the grave in which it lay; Clarke adds any ulcer, sore or leprosy, any cutaneous disorder loathsome or infectious. Wesley points out that the word for the uncleanness of man covers women equally.

Calvin faces the severity head on rather than softening it. He grants it was never lawful to eat polluted flesh, but says that in the sacrifices there was a special reason, since the uncleanness there amounted to sacrilege; hence the burning of the flesh, exactly as with what had outlasted its legitimate time. As for the cutting off, he reports that some have found the sentence so cruel or immoderately severe that they take it to mean no more than being cast out of the camp. He does not follow them. It is not to be wondered at, he says, that God should have dealt so severely with those who knowingly and wilfully contaminated what was holy — since a man who sinned in error did not receive this sentence at all, and it fell only on the one who had betrayed open contempt of God by profaning sacred things.
22:
Ellicott reads the new formula as marking a fresh communication, and the section it opens as doing to the earlier rule about fat and blood what the preceding section did to the rules about the sacrifices — supplementing and expanding a law already given. Gill puts it as a reminder, the laws about fat and blood being repeated to the people.

The prohibition on fat is narrower than it looks, and every voice here narrows it the same way. Wesley confines the general rule to the kinds of creature that were sacrificed, the fat of others being lawful food. Clarke gives the reason — ox, sheep and goat were the only animals offered, though many others ranked as clean — and adds that the ban cannot extend to fat in general, since fat was among the blessings God gave the people, the butter of kine and milk of sheep with the fat of lambs and rams of Bashan being the very provision he made for them. Ellicott agrees that the fat of the three sacrificial kinds was forbidden even when they were killed for private eating, while that of stags, roes and other clean beasts was allowed, and reports the three fats for which the second Temple held a man liable to excision: the fat on the inwards, on the two kidneys, and on the flanks. He also notes the finer distinctions that grew up around the rule — the fat covered with flesh lawful, the fat on the kidneys forbidden, the fat within the kidneys and that of the heart lawful again.

Calvin looks for the purpose rather than the boundary. The fat was consecrated to God in every sacrifice and burnt on the altar, and forbidding it at ordinary meals meant that piety was cultivated at home as well: those far from the temple would be reminded of God's service at their daily table. He knows the allegorical readings other interpreters indulge in here, and declines them, preferring to rest in the reason God himself gives, that the fat was assigned to him.

The fat of a beast that died of itself or was torn is treated as a separate case. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that it might be applied to any common purpose of ordinary life — candles, Ellicott suggests — though never eaten, the carcase being unclean. Wesley heads off an objection: since the flesh of such an animal was itself forbidden, the clause looks superfluous, but the earlier prohibition he takes to have bound the priests only.

Blood is prohibited more broadly and more absolutely. Ellicott would render the clause as binding on Israelites wherever they dwelt, and extends it to all fowls and quadrupeds whether or not they were prescribed for sacrifice, while leaving fishes and creeping things outside it. Gill takes it to cover clean creatures as much as unclean, and reports the Jewish reading of the law as aimed at the limb torn from a living beast and eaten with the blood in it. Clarke reads the cutting off as excommunication from the people of God, and so a loss of any part in their inheritance and their blessings. Ellicott adds the later refinement: excision was inflicted only for the life-blood, the blood in which the life resides and whose loss causes death, while for blood found in the limbs or elsewhere in the body a sin offering was brought and the offender beaten.
28:
Ellicott marks the formula as introducing yet another communication, regulating God's portion of the peace offering. What strikes Henry, Wesley and Ellicott alike is the offerer performing the presentation himself, with no leave to depute it. Wesley describes the mechanics: once the beast was killed and jointed, the priest laid the appointed portions on the offerer's hands and then supported and guided them throughout. Henry reads the two motions as two confessions — the lifting up in token of regard to God as the God of heaven, the waving to and fro in token of regard to him as Lord of the whole earth, the man reaching as far as he could and showing his readiness to do God honour.

Ellicott sets out the whole rite as it stood in the time of Christ, and the sequence is exact. The offerer killed the victim and the priest sprinkled the blood; the animal was flayed, the inwards taken out, the flesh cut up and the breast and right shoulder separated. The priest then laid the fat on the owner's hands, the breast upon it, the shoulder over that, the two kidneys and the caul of the liver above them, the bread on top of all; slipping his own hand beneath the offerer's, he waved everything before the Lord, and afterwards salted the inwards and burned them. He notes provisions for cases outside the pattern: two men in partnership had one wave for both, and a woman's oblation was waved by the priest, since women might do so only in the trial of jealousy and the vow of a Nazarite.

One phrase gives Wesley pause: these are called offerings made by fire, though only part of them went into it. He takes the name loosely rather than strictly, as it is used of a whole burnt sacrifice, since portions here were reserved for the priesthood — yet it holds, because even these were consumed in part.

The division then runs three ways. Gill itemises what the fire took — the fat on the inwards, the two kidneys, the flanks, the caul and the liver — and identifies the priest with the claim on the shoulder as the one who had sprinkled the blood round about the altar and burnt the fat upon it, both rites already enjoined. The fat was burnt on the altar; the breast, waved, became Aaron's and his sons'; the right shoulder, heaved, went to the particular priest who had sprinkled the blood and burnt the fat. Keil and Delitzsch read the arrangement as tribute: God levied these two portions on Israel out of their own peace offerings and made them over to Aaron's house as a right claimable for all ages. Ellicott adds that the perpetual statute binds Israel as long as the priesthood lasts, and that what the priests could not consume of the bread and flesh passed to the owner and his friends. Wesley extends the grant beyond Aaron, to the portion of every succeeding high priest and his family.

Both men look for a meaning in the particular parts chosen. Wesley takes the one for the seat of wisdom and the other for strength in action, and finds in the pair the wisdom and power that were in Christ as high priest and that ought to be in everyone who serves at an altar. Henry's version is directed at the congregation instead: they intimate the affections and the deeds, which all God's people must devote to his honour and all his ministers to the service of the church.
35:
The word portion carries more weight here than it looks. Gill takes the anointing to stand for the office it conferred, so that what follows is the part allotted to Aaron for executing it, and reports Aben Ezra's stronger reading, that it is the reward of his faithful performance — the wave breast and heave shoulder, a cake out of each of the unleavened kinds together with the leavened bread, and the other perquisites of the other offerings besides. Wesley makes the figure explicit and doubles it: the anointing is put for the priesthood, the sign standing for the thing signified, and then put again for the share of the sacrifices which belonged to the priest by virtue of that anointing. Ellicott cuts through the figure altogether and would render it simply the share of Aaron and the share of his sons — meaning the wave breast and the heave shoulder.

Henry reads the two verses as a grant, and reads the timing as part of the point. On the very day they were ordained to the work, provision was made for their comfortable maintenance; God will see to it that those employed for him are well paid and well provided for. He carries the principle forward without softening the terms: those who receive the anointing of the Spirit to minister to the Lord shall have their portion, and a worthy one, out of the offerings of the Lord — since God's work is its own wages, and there is a present reward of obedience in obedience itself.

The obligation runs the other way too. Ellicott makes the command binding on every offerer, who must give the named parts to the officiating priests because they are theirs by right of office; Gill puts the same thing from the priests' side, that whenever the people brought their offerings to be presented, such parts were ordered to be allowed them. Henry turns it into a statute for the people: they were to bring their offerings by the rules prescribed and give the priests their share out of them cheerfully, since the solemn acts of religious worship are commanded and not left to anyone's pleasure. Clarke refers the day of the anointing back to the account of the consecration itself, and Keil and Delitzsch treat these two verses as the hinge on which the instructions about the peace offerings turn into the closing summary of the whole sacrificial law.
37:
The last two verses gather everything up, and Ellicott indexes them item by item — burnt offering, meat offering, sin offering and trespass offering each traced to the chapter that describes it and to the supplement that expands it, and the peace offering to its own two supplements here. Over one term he differs from Wesley. Ellicott would read the consecrations as the offering of consecration, meaning the meat offering the high priest brings on entering the pontifical office; Wesley takes it for the sacrifice offered at the consecration of the priests generally. Keil and Delitzsch note that the fill-offering appears in the summary although it was not instituted in these chapters at all but earlier, and explain the name from the phrase about filling the hand.

Where the laws were given is disputed more sharply. Gill argues that in mount Sinai should be by or near the mount, since these laws were not delivered on the mountain but after the tabernacle had been erected and out of it; the Targum of Jonathan, he notes, paraphrases it as in the tabernacle they made for him in the wilderness of Sinai. He enters a careful qualification too: the verse speaks of the command given in the wilderness to offer sacrifices, not of sacrifices actually offered there. Clarke takes the opposite view, that the laws were probably given while Moses was on the mount with God, the time being ample since he was there fourscore days in all, forty at the giving of the law and forty at its renewing.

Calvin finds the point of a summary in what it forecloses. Moses is indicating that full provision had been made against any addition insinuating itself from men's inventions to vitiate the sacrifices: on the day God appointed them he omitted nothing that was to be observed, so that no one should dare introduce anything he had not prescribed. From so careful an embrace of all the ceremonies he infers how earnestly all temerity in invention is to be avoided, and takes the brief closing admonition as an exhortation to soberness, lest the people transgress the limits God had set.

Clarke uses the summary as the occasion for a glossary of the terms, and several of his derivations carry his reading of the rite with them. The trespass offering he traces to a root meaning to be guilty or liable to punishment, the guilt being reckoned as transferred to the animal and the offerer redeemed from the penalty — and he sets beside it the servant who makes his soul an offering for sin. The sin offering he derives from a verb meaning to miss the mark, which he calls very apt: a sinner is continually aiming at happiness, and because he does not seek it in God the Scripture represents him as missing his aim. The offering was at once an acknowledgment of guilt in having forsaken the fountain of living waters for cisterns that could hold none, and of a firm purpose to return. Atonement he traces to a root meaning to cover or smear over; the meat offering to one meaning to rest after toil, naming the ease a man had when the fruits of autumn were in; the freewill offering to a root meaning to be free, liberal, princely, an offering not commanded but given as proof of extraordinary gratitude. The festival he derives from a verb meaning to dance round in circles, and guesses that the circular dance was meant to figure the revolution of the heavenly bodies and the exact return of the seasons — distinguishing it from the appointed annual feast, which commemorated a particular deliverance. The drink offering he takes from a root meaning to pour out, water or wine poured at the conclusion of a treaty, and reads it as typifying the blood shed for the sin of the world.
